channel.title: 404 Memory Found
channel.description: 404 Memory Found is a nostalgia blog of long-form stories about the technology, games, websites and companies of the 90s and 2000s, wrapped in a Windows 95 desktop.

item.title: What Happened to the Sega Channel, the Cable Service That Streamed Games in 1994
item.description: Before Xbox Game Pass, before the App Store, before broadband was even a word people used, Sega tried to deliver video games to your Genesis through your cable TV box. For a hot minute in the mid '90s, it almost worked.

item.title: What Happened to HyperCard, the Apple Software That Quietly Invented the Web
item.description: In 1987 Apple shipped a program with every Macintosh that let anyone build clickable, multimedia documents with no programming experience required. It was called HyperCard, and almost everything you do on the internet today is a copy of it.

item.title: What Happened to the Sega 32X: The Add-On That Broke Sega
item.description: In November 1994, Sega asked you to bolt a second console on top of your Genesis. It sold 665,000 units, then died in eighteen months. Here is the story.

item.title: The First Banner Ad: How One Click on October 27, 1994 Built the Modern Web
item.description: On October 27, 1994, an AT&T banner ad ran on HotWired with a 44 percent click-through rate. Three decades later, every website you use is shaped by what happened that day.

item.title: What Happened to the Game Genie, the $50 Cheat Device That Beat Nintendo in Court
item.description: Galoob's Game Genie sat between a NES cartridge and the console and lied about how many lives Mario had. Nintendo sued. Galoob won. A whole modding generation was born from a $50 plastic sleeve and a six-letter code.

item.title: What Happened to Geocaching, the GPS Treasure Hunt That Started With a Bucket and a Can of Beans
item.description: When the US military stopped degrading civilian GPS signals on May 1, 2000, a hobbyist in Oregon hid a bucket in the woods the next day. That bucket became geocaching, a 3-million-cache, 191-country platform with a 25-year run.

item.title: What Happened to the Nintendo Power Glove: 1989's Worst Best Toy
item.description: Mattel's Power Glove promised motion-controlled NES gaming in 1989. It barely worked, only two games supported it, and somehow it became one of the most beloved failures in video game history.

item.title: What Happened to theGlobe.com: The Biggest IPO Pop in History
item.description: In 1998 two Cornell undergrads took theGlobe.com public and watched the stock pop 606 percent on day one. It remains the largest first-day gain in IPO history. Here's the full story of how it happened and why it collapsed.

item.title: What Happened to the Atari Lynx, the Color Handheld That Lost to Game Boy
item.description: In 1989, the Atari Lynx had a backlit color screen, hardware sprite scaling, and 8-player networking. It got crushed by a $90 gray brick called the Game Boy. Here is exactly why.

item.title: What Happened to Excite, the Search Engine That Turned Down Google for $750,000
item.description: In 1999, Excite was worth $35 billion and had the chance to buy Google for $750,000. CEO George Bell said no. The full story is more complicated, and a lot more interesting, than the punchline suggests.

item.title: What Happened to the TurboGrafx-16, NEC's Forgotten 16-Bit Console
item.description: It was the king of Japan, the third option in America, and the console that invented half the things we now take for granted. Then it disappeared.

item.title: What Happened to PointCast and the 1990s Push Technology Boom
item.description: In 1997, News Corporation offered $450 million for a company that delivered headlines through a screensaver. Two years later it sold for $7 million. The full story of push technology's rise and collapse.

item.title: How the Nintendo NES Saved Video Games After the 1983 Crash
item.description: In 1985, American retailers had given up on video games. Then a Japanese toy company shipped a gray plastic box with a robot, called it an entertainment system, and resurrected an entire industry. This is the full story of how the NES pulled gaming back from the dead.

item.title: What Happened to Standalone GPS Devices: TomTom and the Smartphone Killer
item.description: In 2008, the world bought 42 million standalone GPS devices. By 2014, the category was effectively dead. The story of how a free Android feature, a Cold War satellite system, and an $11 billion map data war ended an entire consumer electronics market.

item.title: What Happened to TechTV and The Screen Savers Channel
item.description: ZDTV launched in 1998. Comcast killed it in less than a year after the 2004 G4 merger. Here is how a cable channel built for nerds disappeared, and where its hosts went.

item.title: What Happened to Wine.com and the Internet Wine Wars
item.description: Three companies burned through more than $200M trying to sell wine online between 1995 and 2001. The smallest one ended up owning the Wine.com domain.

item.title: What Happened to the Nokia 3310, the Phone That Refused to Die
item.description: Nokia's 3310 sold 126 million units, became an internet meme for being indestructible, and got resurrected from the grave in 2017. Here is the full story of how a small Finnish company built a phone so good it accidentally turned into a cultural symbol.

item.title: What Happened to NCSA Mosaic, the Browser That Built the World Wide Web
item.description: Before Netscape, before Internet Explorer, there was Mosaic. The browser two students built at a public university in 1993 became the front door to the early web, then quietly disappeared while reshaping the next thirty years of the internet.

item.title: What Happened to the Sega CD, the Add-On That Promised Gaming's Future
item.description: Sega bolted a CD-ROM drive onto the Genesis, charged $299, and promised the future of video games. Here is the messy, fascinating story of how it all went sideways.

item.title: What Happened to Prodigy, the Online Service That Beat AOL to America
item.description: Before AOL, before the web, two of the biggest companies in America spent over a billion dollars trying to teach the country how to go online. Prodigy got there first, then lost everything.
